Dyson’s design and commercial success lent authority to his quest to revive the spirit of invention in Britain. In 1997 he published Against the Odds (cowritten with Giles Coren), an autobiographical account of his persistence in the face of discouragement. The following year he was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire . In 2002 the James Dyson Foundation was established with the aim of encouraging young people to enter engineering through the awarding of prizes and grants.

His idea for an unconventional plastic barrow – with a ball rather than a wheel – ultimately drew James away from the safety and comfort of a salary. He went it alone in 1974.

The Ballbarrow went against the grain and overcame many of the problems with traditional wheelbarrows. It featured the world’s first load-spreading, pneumatic ball instead of a narrow wheel which, together with wide legs, prevented it from sinking into soft ground.

These lessons, learnt on his journey as an inventor over the years, occupy the pages of books James has written.

His first, Doing a Dyson, was written by James and Tony Muranka in 1996, and was promptly followed by his first autobiography, Against the Odds, in 1997.

In 2001, James also wrote A History of Great Inventions, and in 2010 he co-presented the Channel 4 TV series, Genius of Britain.

In 2021, a second autobiography, Invention: A Life, was published and quickly entered The Sunday Times bestseller list.
